Redundant SSL configuration overrides connection settings. The top-level `ssl: useSSL` property conflicts with the more specific `ssl` object defined inside the `extra` options. When `useSSL` is true, the top-level `ssl: true` property will override the `extra.ssl` object, which contains `rejectUnauthorized: false`. The underlying `node-postgres` driver will receive `ssl: true`, which defaults to `rejectUnauthorized: true`. This will cause database connection failures in any environment that relies on self-signed certificates, which is the exact scenario `rejectUnauthorized: false` is intended to support. Removing the top-level `ssl: useSSL` property resolves the conflict, allowing the configuration in `extra` to correctly enable or disable SSL with the intended options.

```typescript
            extra: {
                max: poolConfig.max,
                min: poolConfig.min,
                idleTimeoutMillis: 30000,
                connectionTimeoutMillis: 60000,
                keepAlive: true,
                ...(useSSL
                    ? {
                          ssl: {
                              rejectUnauthorized: false,
                          },
                      }
                    : {}),
            },
```

<summary>Prompt for LLM</summary>

```

File libs/core/infrastructure/database/typeorm/typeORM.factory.ts:

Line 69 to 83:

The provided TypeScript code configures a TypeORM database connection for PostgreSQL. It sets a top-level `ssl` property to a boolean value (`useSSL`) and also conditionally sets a more detailed `ssl` object within the `extra` options object. In TypeORM's PostgreSQL driver, top-level properties often override properties within the `extra` object during configuration merging. Explain why this dual configuration is problematic. Specifically, describe what happens when `useSSL` is `true`, causing `ssl: true` to be set at the top level while `extra.ssl` is set to `{ rejectUnauthorized: false }`. Detail which setting takes precedence and what the final effective SSL configuration passed to the `node-postgres` driver will be. Explain the impact of this on database connections that require `rejectUnauthorized: false`, such as those using self-signed certificates.

Suggested Code:

            extra: {
                max: poolConfig.max,
                min: poolConfig.min,
                idleTimeoutMillis: 30000,
                connectionTimeoutMillis: 60000,
                keepAlive: true,
                ...(useSSL
                    ? {
                          ssl: {
                              rejectUnauthorized: false,
                          },

                    : {}),

Veredicto: Sugestão CORRETA, relevância MÉDIA.

  O bug é real. Na linha 102, quando getMCPPlugins() falha com qualquer erro que não seja MCPServiceUnavailableError (ex: network timeout, 500, erro de parse), o código retorna true — ou seja, trata o
  serviço como disponível. Isso pode fazer a UI mostrar a tab/seção de MCP plugins mesmo quando o serviço está inacessível, levando a erros na interface quando o usuário tentar interagir.

  A lógica correta é: se não conseguiu chamar o serviço, independente do tipo de erro, ele não está disponível → retornar false.

  Além disso, a linha 93 tem = true como default do useQuery, o que significa que enquanto a query carrega, assume que MCP está disponível. Isso é discutível mas menos grave (é preferência de UX — mostrar
  otimisticamente ou não).

  Classificação: média relevância — não é um crash, mas causa comportamento incorreto na UI (mostrar funcionalidade indisponível). Faz sentido corrigir.

Veredicto: Sugestão CORRETA, relevância MÉDIA-BAIXA.

  O bug descrito é real: se businessLogic feature flag mudar de false para true depois do mount, o initializedRef.current já é true e o useEffect não roda novamente para adicionar business_logic ao
  mergedOptions.

  A solução proposta resolve: remove a ref e usa hasChanges para só chamar setValue quando há labels novas. Isso é idempotente — se visibleAllLabels mudar (flag ativada), adiciona a label que falta sem
  resetar as existentes.

  Porém, na prática o impacto é baixo porque:
  - Feature flags normalmente não mudam durante a sessão do usuário — são carregados uma vez no boot
  - Se o flag mudar, o usuário provavelmente vai recarregar a página
  - O cenário real mais provável seria: flag ativo desde o início → funciona normal, flag inativo → business_logic nem aparece na UI

  Classificação: média-baixa relevância — é um edge case legítimo mas improvável no uso real. A correção é limpa e melhora a robustez sem downside.

Vulnerabilidade no processo de build. A instrução `COPY . .` na linha 18 sobrescreve o diretório `node_modules` criado pela etapa `RUN yarn install` na linha 15. Se um desenvolvedor construir a imagem com um diretório `node_modules` local presente (um cenário comum), os módulos do host (potencialmente compilados para um SO diferente, como macOS ou Windows) substituirão os módulos compatíveis com Linux dentro da imagem. Isso fará com que a aplicação falhe em tempo de execução ao tentar carregar addons nativos, quebrando o cenário de fallback mencionado no novo comentário.

```dockerfile
# Copy all source code first to ensure a clean slate
COPY . .

# Install dependencies based on the copied source code.
# This is safer as it avoids overwriting with host node_modules.
RUN yarn install --frozen-lockfile
```

<summary>Prompt for LLM</summary>

```

File docker/Dockerfile.web.dev:

Line 15 to 18:

Estou revisando um Dockerfile para um ambiente de desenvolvimento Node.js. A ordem atual das instruções é `COPY package.json`, depois `RUN yarn install`, e finalmente `COPY . .`. O problema é que o `COPY . .` sobrescreve o diretório `node_modules` que foi instalado dentro do contêiner com o diretório `node_modules` da máquina host, se ele existir. Isso causa falhas de tempo de execução devido a binários incompatíveis (por exemplo, macOS vs. Linux). Proponha uma correção para este Dockerfile que resolva o problema de sobrescrita, garantindo que a imagem resultante seja sempre executável, mesmo que isso implique um trade-off de desempenho no cache de camadas do Docker.

Suggested Code:

COPY . .

# Install dependencies based on the copied source code.
# This is safer as it avoids overwriting with host node_modules.
RUN yarn install --frozen-lockfile

Veredicto: Sugestão INCORRETA / prejudicial.

  O Dockerfile atual segue o padrão correto e canônico de Docker:

  1. COPY package.json yarn.lock → layer de dependências
  2. RUN yarn install → instala deps (cached se package.json não mudou)
  3. COPY . . → copia source code

  A sugestão inverte para COPY . . → RUN yarn install, o que:
  - Mata o cache de layers do Docker — qualquer mudança em qualquer arquivo do source code invalida o cache e reinstala todas as dependências do zero. Isso transforma builds de segundos em minutos.
  - O problema de "host node_modules sobrescrevendo" é resolvido de outras formas mais corretas:
    - .dockerignore com node_modules (a solução padrão e correta)
    - Volume mount no docker-compose que exclui node_modules

⏺ Searched for 1 pattern (ctrl+o to expand)

⏺ Confirmado — .dockerignore já tem node_modules e **/node_modules. O COPY . . nunca copia node_modules do host para dentro do container. O problema que a sugestão descreve não existe.

  Classificação: ignorar — a sugestão é baseada numa premissa falsa (o .dockerignore já resolve) e a "correção" degradaria significativamente o tempo de build

Veredicto: Sugestão CORRETA, relevância MÉDIA.

  O cenário descrito é real:

  1. Execução 1: Usuário tem regras de negócio no PR body → businessLogicPrBodyHash = 'abc123' → salvo como businessLogicHash: 'abc123' no DB
  2. Execução 2: Usuário remove as regras do PR body → businessLogicPrBodyHash é undefined (nunca é setado no context) → if (result.businessLogicPrBodyHash) é falsy → o hash antigo 'abc123' permanece no DB
  3. Execução 3+: O código compara lastHash === currentHash (linha 531). Como lastHash ainda é 'abc123' do DB e não existe PR body com signals, currentHash seria diferente → a verificação falha corretamente
   nesse caso específico porque hasBusinessSignals (linha 524) retorna false antes de chegar ao check do hash.

  Porém, há um cenário mais sutil: se o usuário muda o conteúdo das regras de negócio, depois remove, depois adiciona de volta o mesmo texto original — o hash antigo stale faria o dedup achar que "já
  processou" e pular a análise.

  A correção com 'businessLogicPrBodyHash' in result resolve: quando a propriedade existe com valor null/undefined, salva null no DB, limpando o hash obsoleto.

  Classificação: média relevância — é um bug de dados stale que pode causar skip indevido de análise de business logic em edge cases. Não é catastrófico mas é um bug lógico legítimo.

messages.text: Intentional — kept the lowest breakpoint and documented why in 11f8e7744. The read applies a tier as a **per-call binary** (a call above the threshold is priced entirely at the tier rate, else at default; not graduated). With one breakpoint, the lowest one elevates the widest set of large calls: everything above the first tier. Picking the highest breakpoint would instead leave the whole first-tier band (e.g. 200k–1M) priced at the *default* rate, underpricing a far more common range than the ultra-rare calls above a second breakpoint. Also moot today: every tiered model in use has exactly one context tier (>200k), so this is a tiebreak of one.

messages.author: acoliver
messages.text:
Declining, with the reason this rule cannot apply to this file.

**The suggested code does not compile.** `this.observabilityService` does not exist at module scope in a jest spec — the reference implementation was generated for a class method and pasted into a spec.

**Token accounting for this model happens at the call layer, by design.** Production callers go through `runAiSdkLLMInSpan` at `libs/llm/agent-loop-call.ts:223` and `libs/llm/structured-review-call.ts:328` before reaching this transport. Every product invocation of `chatgpt_subscription` is accounted at those sites; wrapping again inside the transport would double-count each call, and wrapping inside the spec would count nothing at all — the model here is a mock emitting fixture `usage` objects, so a span would record fabricated token consumption and pollute the accounting the rule exists to protect.

**No spec in the repository wraps model calls in spans.** The only references to `runAiSdkLLMInSpan` in spec files are mocks *of* it (`structured-review-call.spec.ts:65`, `observability.service.spec.ts:111`) testing the callers of the accounting layer, never the calls under test.

messages.author: malinosqui
messages.text:
Declining this one, with the reason.

`apps/web` has no Pino. There is no `PinoLoggerService` in the Next app and no `pino` dependency in its package.json — that service lives in the Nest side, and importing it into a server action would pull the backend DI container into the web bundle. `console.error` is what the web's server code uses, including the eight other call sites in this same file's neighbourhood, so this would be one inconsistent line rather than a fix.

What the rule is actually protecting — an error that reaches the logs with enough context to act on — is covered: each catch here logs the action name and the params that matter. If the web gets a real logger, this file should move with the rest of them in one pass, not on its own.

findSuggestionsByPRAndFilenames unwinds the full accumulated `files[].suggestions` array of every changed file and returns all matching SENT suggestions, with the 5-per-file/30-total caps applied only afterwards in BuildPreviousReviewDecisionsUseCase. Since `files[].suggestions` accumulates one entry per suggestion per review round, on a long-lived PR this aggregation's result set and transferred/memory cost grow linearly with round count on every round of every PR, regardless of the caps — the query cost is bounded by nothing. Push the caps into the aggregation, e.g. sort files.suggestions by createdAt desc and $slice to 5 per file before $unwind (and $limit after), or add a createdAt floor (only suggestions from the last N rounds) to the filter.

{ $addFields: { 'files.suggestions': { $slice: [ { $sortArray: { input: '$files.suggestions', sortBy: { createdAt: -1 } } }, 5 ] } } },
{ $unwind: '$files.suggestions' },
{ $match: { 'files.suggestions.deliveryStatus': deliveryStatus } },

Good catch — that was a real regression in my own fix, and worse than the bug it fixed. Fixed in 5ffec70.

Only a plain object or array is serialized now and written back to the config; `FormData`, `URLSearchParams`, `Blob` and anything else is passed through exactly as the caller built it, so the payload survives. ```

The newly exposed `prState` filter is a coarse post-query in-memory filter applied at get-enriched-pull-requests.use-case.ts:~661 inside the keyset loop, whose only exits are `enrichedPullRequests.length < limit` and `hasMoreExecutions`, so with no iteration cap a request can keep issuing sequential Mongo queries until the whole execution history is drained. messages.author: malinosqui
messages.text:
Fixed in 992895714 — the cap landed in `get-enriched-pull-requests.use-case.ts` rather than in this DTO, which is why this thread stayed anchored here.

The page-filling loop had only two exits, `enrichedPullRequests.length < limit` and `hasMoreExecutions`, so any selective post-query filter could keep it issuing sequential batches. It now also stops at `MAX_BATCHES_PER_REQUEST` (10).

A capped request returns a short page with `hasMoreExecutions` still true, so it still hands back a cursor. That is safe here because the client continues on the cursor alone and never on page length — `getNextPageParam` in `apps/web/src/lib/services/pull-requests/hooks.ts` returns `pagination.nextCursor` and explicitly ignores how many rows came back, so a short or empty page does not end the list.

Source rows with `status: 'infra'` are discarded from the queue and never re-emitted, yet the output reports `cases: rows.length` and `infraFailures` counting only newly-detected failures. The rejudged file silently describes a different population than the run it re-scores, so a nightly whose summary had 30 cases with 3 infra now produces 27 cases and `infraFailures: 0`, misleading the calibration and compare tooling. const carriedInfra = (original.rows || []).filter((row) => row.status === 'infra').map((row) => ({ caseId: row.caseId, status: 'infra', reason: 'infra in source run' }));

messages.text:
Valid rule, fixed in 3d195bca8 — the pass now builds one index keyed `${projectId}|${repoId}|${eventType}`, the same key the prune step groups by, so the two cannot disagree about what counts as the same subscription, and the lookup is a `get`.

One correction to the reasoning: the cost was real but small. For 200 repositories the scan was 600 lookups over a snapshot of roughly the same size — a few hundred thousand comparisons, sub-millisecond. The listing was the expensive part of this pass, not the scanning. Worth doing for the rule and because the shared key removes a way for the two sides to drift, not for the runtime.

messages.author: Kody
Wellington01
messages.text:
Valid, fixed in 3d195bca8. The listing is the single input the whole pass reads, so losing it means nothing is created and nothing is pruned for any repository — that deserves its own catch and its own message rather than surfacing through the pass-level one, which cannot say which step failed. It now logs the repository count it gave up on and returns instead of throwing, which keeps the fire-and-forget caller intact.

I did not add the retry. With one call per pass instead of 3 per repository, the odds of hitting a transient limit here are far lower than what the old code faced, and a save is user-initiated and repeatable. Worth revisiting if the logs show it happening.

Four tests cover it: no writes anywhere when the listing fails, the promise never rejects, and the single-flight guard is released so the next save still runs.

Valid, and this is the best catch of the five — fixed in 46797365c. The old code deleted and recreated on every save, so it healed a disabled subscription as a side effect; skipping redundant work turned that accident into a hole. Confirmed against the reported organization, which already has subscriptions sitting in a restricted state.

Took the suggestion as written on both sides: `usable` now requires health, and the duplicate collapse prefers a keeper that is both delivering and carrying a valid token, so it can no longer keep a disabled copy and delete the enabled one beside it. Missing status reads as enabled, so an unexpected response shape causes no churn.

Seven tests added, five of which fail against the previous behaviour: one per Azure status (`onProbation`, `disabledBySystem`, `disabledByUser`, `disabledByInactiveIdentity`), the enabled and missing-status cases as guards against churn, and the duplicate case with one dead copy and one live one.

Valid, and it was a real defect in this branch — fixed in 799522635.

Confirmed the mechanism: `existing` was the first URL match, ownership was only checked afterwards, and `createOrReplaceHook` deletes `existing` when it is not usable. So another team's entry sorted ahead of ours got deleted, and because our own healthy marked copy was never examined, the pass then created a second one beside it — Azure delivering every event twice.

Took the suggestion as written: ownership is resolved first, coverage is decided from the owned copy regardless of listing order, and the only subscription that can be replaced is one this pass may remove (ours, or an unmarked one predating the marker). Another team's is left untouched.

One correction to the report: the 429/403 branch does not leave the repository uncovered. Our own healthy subscription was still present the whole time — it was simply ignored. The harm was the duplicate, not a coverage gap.

Two tests, both failing against the previous code: our healthy subscription is treated as coverage with a foreign entry sorted first, and a foreign subscription is never deleted to make room for ours.

```bash
step "Impersonation: grant before flipping the variables, revoke after"
for repo in "${WRITER_REPOS[@]}"; do
  gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding "$WRITER_SA" --role=roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser --member="$(member_of "$repo")" --quiet >/dev/null && echo "$repo -> $WRITER"
done
for repo in "${PULL_REPOS[@]}"; do
  gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding "$PULL_SA" --role=roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser --member="$(member_of "$repo")" --quiet >/dev/null && echo "$repo -> $PULL"
done

step "GitHub repo variables"
for repo in "${WRITER_REPOS[@]}"; do set_vars "$repo" "$WRITER_SA"; done
for repo in "${PULL_REPOS[@]}"; do set_vars "$repo" "$PULL_SA"; done

step "Revoke the old writer identity from the pull repos (last, variables already flipped)"
for repo in "${PULL_REPOS[@]}"; do

`docker/Dockerfile.web.dev` sets `pnpm_config_verify_deps_before_run=false`, but unlike `docker/Dockerfile.dev` there is no dep-sync replacement here: the web image has no ENTRYPOINT (CMD `pnpm start:dev`, no `command:`/`entrypoint:` in the web service) and `apps/web` is bind-mounted, so `web_node_modules_cache` is only seeded once during build and never re-synced. After any `apps/web` dependency change, `pnpm start:dev` will run `next dev` against the stale volume (module-not-found) and crash-loop under `restart: unless-stopped`, with recovery limited to the manual, destructive `docker volume rm kodus-ai_web_node_modules_cache` (`apps/web` script `docker:clean-cache`; `docker:reset` does not remove volumes) — the pre-run verification was the only auto-heal, and the memory-cap rationale in the comment does not hold for web (its cap is 4G in `docker-compose.dev.yml` and 8G in `docker-compose.preview.yml`, not the 1G that OOM-killed mcp-manager). Of course. Here is a breakdown of the problem:

**The Core Issue:**
The new logic incorrectly applies rules because it only checks if the rule and the code being analyzed are at the same *level* (e.g., both are 'directory' level), but it fails to check if they are for the *same specific directory*.

This causes the system to bypass important inheritance controls like `inheritable: false` and `exclude` lists.

**Step-by-Step Example of the Bug:**

Imagine this setup:
*   **Parent Directory Rule:** A rule is set for `directory A` and is marked as **not inheritable** (`inheritable: false`).
*   **File Location:** You are checking a file inside `directory B`, which is a child of `directory A`.

Here's what happens with the faulty code:
1.  The system checks the level of the file's location (`directory B`). The level is `'directory'`. 
2.  It then checks the level of the rule (for `directory A`). That level is also `'directory'`. 
3.  The new code has a check: `if (ruleLevel === currentLevel)`. In this case, `'directory' === 'directory'`, which is `true`.
4.  The function immediately returns `true`, incorrectly deciding that the rule applies.

**The Consequence:**
The rule from the parent directory (`directory A`) is applied to the child (`directory B`), completely ignoring the `inheritable: false` setting. The logic that should have prevented this is skipped entirely.

messages.text:
You've pointed out a great function, `isRepositoryMatch(rule)`, but it addresses a different part of the problem than the bug I found.

Let me clarify the two separate checks that happen:

1.  **`isRepositoryMatch(rule)`**: This function's job is to check if the rule is defined for the correct repository. This is a broad, initial check. For example, if we are analyzing a file in `repository A`, this ensures we don't accidentally use a rule specifically created for `repository B`.

2.  **The Buggy Logic (inside `isInheritanceMatch`)**: The issue I flagged is *after* we've already confirmed the rule is in the right repository. The problem is with how the rule is applied to **subdirectories**. The faulty code (`if (ruleLevel === currentLevel)`) incorrectly applies a rule from a parent directory to a child directory, even when the rule is marked as non-inheritable (`inheritable: false`).

In short, `isRepositoryMatch` validates the **repository scope**, while the bug is in the logic that handles **directory inheritance**. Because they control two different aspects of rule validation, `isRepositoryMatch` cannot fix the inheritance bug.

That's a great question. You're right that `isPathMatch` is a key part of the overall validation, but it addresses a different concern than `isInheritanceMatch`, and unfortunately, it doesn't solve the inheritance bug.

Here’s a breakdown of their distinct roles:

1.  **`isPathMatch(rule)`**: This function checks if the file being analyzed (e.g., `src/components/Button.js`) matches the path patterns defined in the rule (e.g., `path: 'src/components/**'`). It answers the question: *"Does this rule care about this specific file path?"*

2.  **`isInheritanceMatch(rule)`**: This function determines if a rule defined for a broader scope (like a parent directory or the entire repository) should be applied to the current, more specific context (like a child directory). It answers the question: *"Is this rule allowed to apply here based on inheritance settings?"*

The bug I pointed out is entirely **inside** the `isInheritanceMatch` function. The faulty logic `if (ruleLevel === currentLevel)` incorrectly returns `true` *before* it has a chance to check the actual inheritance settings like `inheritable: false` or `exclude` arrays.

So, even if `isPathMatch` returns `true`, the execution still proceeds to `isInheritanceMatch`, where the bug causes the rule to be applied incorrectly, breaking the inheritance logic.

1. compressAndEncrypt é CPU-bound (compressão + criptografia), não I/O-bound. Em Node.js single-threaded, paralelizar operações CPU-bound com Promise.all não dá ganho real — as promises vão rodar
  intercaladas no mesmo event loop, não em paralelo de verdade.
  2. O ganho seria mínimo — cada compressAndEncrypt provavelmente leva microsegundos/milissegundos. O gargalo real dessa função é o this.initializeTask (HTTP POST) e o awaitTask (polling com backoff) logo
  abaixo na linha 101-109.
  3. Risco de pico de memória — com Promise.all, todos os arquivos do batch seriam comprimidos e encriptados simultaneamente na memória. O loop sequencial processa um de cada vez, mantendo o uso de memória
  mais estável. Considerando que já estamos cuidando de memória nesse pipeline, não faz sentido ir na contramão.
  4. O código atual já usa Promise.all internamente (linha 83-86) para paralelizar content + diff do mesmo arquivo, que é o nível certo de paralelismo.

  Veredicto: ignorar. O ganho é negligível para CPU-bound em Node single-threaded, e vai contra o trabalho de otimização de memória que fizemos. Pode mandar a próxima.

messages.text:
O argumento é correto: se um validator é fornecido e nenhum bloco passa, o código cai no fallback do último bloco — que sabemos que não passou no validator. Porém:

  O fallback é intencional. O comentário na linha 106 diz explicitamente: // No validator OR none passed → last valid block (current behavior).

  A lógica é: "tente achar o bloco certo, mas se não conseguir, retorne alguma coisa parseável em vez de nada". O caller (LLMResponseProcessor.processResponse) já tem tratamento para quando o resultado não
  tem codeSuggestions — ele loga o erro e retorna null.

  Se adicionarmos return null quando o validator falha, perdemos a chance de recuperar dados parciais. E o caller que passa o validator é justamente o processResponse que valida
  Array.isArray(obj?.codeSuggestions) — se nenhum bloco tem codeSuggestions, retornar o último bloco não causa dano (vai retornar um objeto sem codeSuggestions, e o caller trata com
  parsedResponse?.codeSuggestions || []).

  Veredicto: ignorar. O fallback é defensivo por design — "melhor retornar algo parseável do que null". Se cortarmos, perdemos resiliência sem ganho prático.

messages.author: malinosqui
messages.text:
Not applying this one — the mechanism you describe is right, the conclusion isn't.

You're correct that `Boolean('')` is false, so an entry whose title is an empty string is dropped and `rulesCount` shrinks with it. That part is accurate. But dropping it is the intended behaviour, not a slip:

- The suggested fix lets `''` through, which renders as a **blank bullet** in the email and still counts toward the "N new rules" headline. That's a worse artifact than the omission — the reader sees an empty line item and no way to tell what it was.
- Keeping the filter as-is means the list and the count always tell the same story. Under the suggested version they can disagree in a way nobody can debug from the email.
- The scenario also can't be reached from the producer: `generate-kody-rules.use-case.ts` sends `createdRules.map((r) => r.title)`, and those titles come from rules that were already created and persisted.

What was genuinely missing is that **nothing in the code said any of this** — you had to infer the empty-string case from `Boolean(entry)`, which is exactly what made it read as accidental. Fixed in edc20d41b: the docblock now states the empty-title drop and why, and there's a test pinning it.

For future reviews, the useful distinction here: when a guard's behaviour is deliberate but undocumented, the defect is the missing intent, not the guard. Flagging "this is unstated, make it explicit" would have landed; "change the filter" would have introduced the bug it was trying to prevent.

messages.author: malinosqui
messages.text:
Not taking this one — the sequencing is deliberate, and I should have said so in a comment.

The two listings share one budget (`budget.kept`), and the walk stops when that budget is filled. Sequentially, review comments get first claim on it, which is what we want: they carry the `path` the comment was left on, and that path is what replaces the per-PR files call this PR removes. Run in parallel, the split between the two sources depends on which pages return first, so the sample that feeds rule generation becomes nondeterministic — the same repo could produce different rules run to run for no reason anyone could trace.

The latency this trades away is one extra round trip on a background onboarding job, so there is no user waiting on it.

Adding a comment at the call site explaining the ordering, so the next reader does not have to rediscover it.

This suggestion is wrong, and following it is what broke the feature.

`$$REMOVE` inside a `$group` `$push` accumulator does skip the element — it does not store a null. Same pipeline as this PR's, against mongo 8.2, first file being `[NOT_SENT, SENT, SENT]`:

```
with $$REMOVE  -> [{"firstSent":[{"id":"sugg-0-1","filePath":"src/file0.ts"}]}]
```

So the original code in 149da7d5 (`$$REMOVE` + `firstSent: 1` + `row.firstSent[0]`) was already correct.

Acting on this comment, d3c3368 swapped `$$REMOVE` for `null` and added `$slice: ['$firstSent', 1]` in the projection. The `$slice` truncates the array to its first element *before* the mapper's `.filter(Boolean)` can drop the nulls, so any PR whose first unwound suggestion wasn't SENT yielded `[null]` and lost its deep-link target — the common case, since filtered-out suggestions are normal. The integration test added in this same PR (`pullRequests-aggregation.integration.spec.ts`, the `[NOT_SENT, SENT, SENT]` case) fails against it; it only stayed green because the suite self-skips without `TEST_MONGODB_URI`, which CI never set.

Fixed on main.

messages.text: @kody Just a quick question: we have a rule stating that the controller never accesses a service directly—right? It always goes through a use case, and there’s never any business logic inside the controller either. I ask because you mentioned a rule violation here—was that incorrect for this context?

messages.author: Kody
messages.text:
Good question — short answer: no, that flag wasn't incorrect. They're two different rules at two different layers, so they don't cancel each other out:

**1. What I flagged is about wiring, not layering.** "Inject services and repositories via DI tokens, not by class" governs *how* a dependency is provided to whatever consumes it. The controller took `KodusCreditsMeteringService` by its concrete class, so the rule applied — and it's already addressed in the current head: `apps/api/src/controllers/kodusCredits.controller.ts:46` now uses `@Inject(KODUS_CREDITS_METERING_SERVICE_TOKEN)`, with the token defined in `libs/analytics/application/credits/kodus-credits-metering.service.ts:105` and registered in `libs/analytics/modules/kodus-credits.module.ts:48` (same token the sweep cron uses at `apps/api/src/cron/kodusCreditsSweep.cron.ts:27`). Worth noting: moving this call into a use case wouldn't remove that requirement — the use case would `@Inject()` the very same token. So it's not either/or; the wiring fix stands under any layering.

**2. On "controllers go through use cases, no business logic in controllers":** that's the direction in this repo — `apps/api/AGENTS.md` states controllers are thin and business logic lives in use cases — and this controller honors it: `charges()` reads the org from the request, calls `listCharges`, and shapes the response. Just one nuance: direct service use from controllers *for reads* does exist in the codebase (e.g., `notification.controller.ts`, `spendLimit.controller.ts`, `tokenUsage.controller.ts` mix use-cases and services), so the current shape isn't an outlier here.

If the team wants the stricter "reads go through use cases too" convention, that's a separate follow-up — but it wouldn't make the token wiring wrong either way. If there's a rule that pins this down further, link it and I'll apply it on future reviews.

messages.author: malinosqui

Declining: the feature already is behind `@CheckPolicies`, so a dedicated `ResourceType` would add a permission surface without changing who can do what.

Every endpoint that exposes or mutates the Kodus provider is on the organization-parameters controller and guarded by `ResourceType.OrganizationSettings` — the provider list and model list with `Action.Read`, the connection probe and the credential save with `Action.Create`, the config delete with `Action.Delete`. The one new endpoint in this PR, `GET /credits/charges`, is guarded by `ResourceType.Billing` (moved there from `TokenUsage` earlier in this same review, with the RBAC matrix regenerated in 9258b75).

It sits in front of the permission checks, not instead of them. Splitting a new resource out of OrganizationSettings would mean every role policy needs a new grant to keep today's behavior, which is churn with no security gain.

`withSignature` computes the HMAC body as `typeof config?.body === "string" ? config.body : ""`, so any caller that passes an object (or otherwise non-string) body signs an empty body while `fetch` sends the coerced payload, producing a signature that cannot match billing's computation. A body is unsignable only if it has its own byte representation we would have to consume to read it (`FormData`, `URLSearchParams`, `Blob`, `ArrayBuffer` or a view, anything with `getReader`). A body that cannot be signed is a caller bug, and turning it into a silent null is the exact failure mode this signature was added to remove.

messages.author: Wellington01
messages.text: Not applying as suggested — this is a real tension, but the fix isn't just 'compare the sha': the joiner in the overlap case may genuinely need a DIFFERENT commit than what's on disk while the other consumer is still reading, and there's no way to give the joiner a fresh checkout without disturbing that reader on this single shared working tree. Skipping the sync trades 'joiner keeps a stale tree in a narrow window before TTL reap' for 'destructive checkout corrupts an active reader mid-review' — the latter is strictly worse (silent wrong findings vs. a bounded staleness window that self-heals on the next reconnect once the other lease releases). A real fix (per-consumer sandboxes, or tracking the synced sha so a genuinely-stale joiner can force a fresh sandbox instead of joining) is a bigger change than this PR's scope; opening a follow-up issue instead of blocking this fix on it.

Finding accepted, suggested fix not taken — fixed differently in 3d195bca8.

The precondition checks out. `handleIntegration` looks the integration up by (organization, team) and creates one when it finds none, with no check on `orgName`, so nothing stops two teams connecting the same Azure organization — and two teams owning different repositories in one organization is a reasonable setup, not a corner case. Matching on a callback URL that is a single deployment-wide env var is not proof of ownership. This PR introduced that prune, so it introduced the risk.

The suggested fix does not work here. Scoping the prune to `previousRepositories` is what `GithubService` does, but `delete-integration.use-case.ts:96` deletes every integration config row after `deleteWebhook` runs, so after a PAT reset there is no previous selection to compare against and nothing would ever converge. That reset is exactly the path this work exists to support: the reported organization rotates its PAT by resetting the integration and re-selecting repositories.

Instead, ownership is now recorded rather than inferred. A subscription carries the team that minted it in its callback URL (`&team=<teamId>`), and only those are eligible for removal. The webhook controller reads `token` and ignores the rest of the query, so delivery is unaffected, and a team id survives an integration reset where a config row does not.

One subtlety worth flagging for review: ownership is deliberately narrower than the match used when creating. A subscription minted before the marker existed belongs to nobody, so it is never deleted on another team's behalf — but it is still found and replaced when its repository is in the selection, which is what tags it. Ignoring it on the create side would leave it in place and add a second subscription beside it, and Azure would then deliver every event twice.

Five tests, all failing against the previous rule: another team's subscription survives a save that does not include its repository, an unmarked one survives too, an unmarked one for a selected repository is replaced rather than duplicated, created subscriptions carry the marker, and an already-marked one is not rewritten.

messages.author: Kody

messages.text:
Finding accepted and fixed in 799522635; the `previousRepositories` half declined again.

The duplicate-delivery half is right, and checking *why* it is right also settled a question I had been carrying. `WebhookContextService.getContext` resolves the team from `findIntegrationConfigWithTeams(REPOSITORIES, repositoryId, platformType)` — the repository in the database, not anything on the subscription. Since every team on a deployment shares one webhook URL, **one** subscription per repository and event already serves all of them. A second copy is not extra coverage for a second team; it is a second delivery and a second review.

So the `ownedKeys` fold is not just safe, it is the correct reading: collapsing an unmarked copy of a key we own cannot uncover anybody, because the marked copy that proves the key is ours is what stays behind. Implemented, plus the keeper is now chosen by ownership first — otherwise a collapse could discard the marked copy and undo the marking, forcing the next pass to redo it.

One correction to the suggested code: the fold must exclude another team's **marked** subscriptions, which also match the URL and the key. Written as `belongsToTeam(...) || (url.includes(webhookUrl) && ownedKeys.has(key))` it pulls them in and deletes them. My first attempt had exactly that bug and the listing-order test caught it; the condition now also requires the copy to carry no marker at all.

`previousRepositories` still does not work here: `delete-integration.use-case.ts:96` removes every integration config row, so after a PAT reset — the path this work exists to support — there is no previous selection to compare against and nothing would converge. Unmarked hooks for a deselected repository whose key we own no copy of therefore remain, which is the accepted cost stated in the PR body.

Three tests: an unmarked copy of a key we own is collapsed, the marked copy survives the collapse, and an unmarked subscription whose key we own no copy of is still left alone.

The retire guard filters `runo environments` output on `.profile` (`(.profile // "") == ""`), but the payload runo returns has no `profile` key — `src/provider/remote.ts` `SharedEnvironment` is { envName, slug, owner, repo, branch, instanceId, createdAt, recipe?, urls?, services? } and `src/main.ts` `cmdEnvironments` prints exactly that JSON. `(.profile // "") == ""` is therefore true for every env of the branch, so on every push (synchronize/reopened/label) to a PR that already has a preview the step runs `$RUNO destroy --branch "$HEAD_REF" …` and tears down the live VM before `up` recreates it: the seeded DB and sessions are wiped, a new provision costs minutes per push, the sslip.io URL changes (contrary to the promised "a new push wakes it and updates this link"), and the destroy-branch also takes whatever shape envs exist, since destroy is resolved by repo+branch only. remove/guard the retire block until runo exposes a real profile discriminator (e.g. gate it behind the same `--profile` capability preflight, or match on a field the payload actually carries), so it only fires for genuinely pre-profile environments.

```yaml
# only meaningful once runo carries a profile field; without it the filter
# matches every env of the branch and destroys the live preview on each push
if $RUNO environments | jq -e --arg b "$HEAD_REF" \
     'map(select(.repo == "kodus-ai" and .branch == $b and has("profile") and (.profile // "") == "")) | length > 0' >/dev/null; then
  echo "retiring the pre-profile preview of $HEAD_REF"
  $RUNO destroy --branch "$HEAD_REF" --recipe .kodus/workspace.preview.yaml
fi
```

messages.author: Wellington01
messages.text: Real class, fixed — though not exploitable as described. Measured with git 2.51: when two sections claim one path, `submodule init` registers the LAST one and only that one, including on the deep retry's `init -- <path>`. So `resolvedUrls` already describes the section git will use, and the other section arrives with no resolved url and is denied. The attack needs the malicious section to win the tie-break, and the winner is exactly the one validated. That said, it is undocumented behaviour holding up a security boundary, so `decideSubmodules` now refuses any path claimed by more than one section outright.

messages.text: Not taking this one. `configPairs` cannot grow with the number of sections: `sshRewriteFor` only ever emits the key `url.https://<repo host>/.insteadOf`, and the host is the repository's own, so the distinct values are bounded by the ssh prefix forms (`git@host:`, `ssh://git@host/`, `ssh://host/`) — at most four entries including the auth header, whatever `.gitmodules` contains. The loop is O(n) over decisions with a constant-size scan, not O(n^2).

![kody code-review](https://img.shields.io/badge/kody-code--review-312B4B?labelColor=C9BBF2) ![Bug](https://img.shields.io/badge/Bug-B71C1C) ![high](https://img.shields.io/badge/severity_level-high-6B6B92)


`parseSshUrl` only recognizes the scp-like form when the host contains a dot (`scp[2].includes('.')`, line 175), while the `ssh://` branch (line 166) has no such requirement, so the same host is accepted as `ssh://git@gitlab/acme/commons.git` but rejected as `git@gitlab:acme/commons.git`. On a self-hosted install with a single-label hostname the submodule stays unfetched (`decideSubmodules` falls through to `deny('not an http(s) URL (ssh/scp/git/file transport)')`), producing exactly the #1939 false positive this feature exists to remove. Keep the drive/scheme guards as explicit prefix checks instead of requiring a dot, rejecting only when the value is a scheme (`raw.indexOf('://') !== -1`) or a Windows drive form (`/^[A-Za-z]:[\/]/.test(raw)`), and let the existing `ssh.host === repo.host` comparison decide.

messages.author: Wellington01
messages.text: Fixed, and it was the sharper half of this review: a single-label host is ordinary self-hosted (`git@gitlab:acme/x.git`) and the `ssh://` branch never required a dot, so that asymmetry refused exactly the installs the feature exists for. Only a scheme url and a Windows drive are excluded now; the same-host comparison decides the rest.

The added warning is good (metadata now carries organizationAndTeamData, prNumber, repositoryId and jobId), but it sits inside the `if (!platformPr)` branch that still completes the job as a clean success — right after this log the code runs `await this.markCompleted(jobId, { reason: 'PLATFORM_PR_NOT_FOUND' })` and returns, so the execution ends as COMPLETED even though the implementation check never ran. Rule 17 requires a review-pipeline stage that answers "not found" because the upstream call failed or the client was unavailable to record the degraded outcome with severity: 'critical' (output not trustworthy — the check did not run) or severity: 'partial'; logger.warn alone is not enough because it does not change the execution status, so the run finishes as a success and the user sees nothing, the same gap flagged in the previous review round. Keep the early return but record the degradation — for example `await this.markCompleted(jobId, { reason: 'PLATFORM_PR_NOT_FOUND', severity: 'critical' });` (or push the error to context.errors with severity: 'critical') so downstream consumers can tell the verification did not execute instead of seeing a clean success.

messages.author: Wellington01
messages.text: Not changing this one. `JobStatus` has no degraded state (PENDING/PROCESSING/COMPLETED/FAILED/WAITING_FOR_EVENT/CANCELLED), and the existing "PR not in the database" exit (`:105`, `PR_NOT_FOUND`) completes with a reason the same way. FAILED would retry a check that cannot run (PR deleted or not served by the provider), and `severity` on the job result is read by nothing. The outcome is recorded as `reason: PLATFORM_PR_NOT_FOUND` plus the warn with org, PR, repository and job.

Wellington01
messages.text: Not changing this one. For the same name the search returns the same candidates, so re-querying on every review yields the same null and only pays the call again. That is what happened before this PR, on every review. Matching case-insensitively would change which account an author resolves to, and display names are not unique, so it belongs in its own change.
